METHODS OF TEACHING


               CHAPTER ONE
Introduction to Teaching and the Subject as a Discipline


                   Postgraduate Study Edition

Chapter One — Introduction to Teaching and the Subject as a Discipline




Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, students should be able to:

  1. Define teaching and distinguish the transmission view of instruction from the facilitation
     (constructivist-influenced) view.
  2. List and explain the basic functions a teacher performs before, during, and after instruction, and
     relate these to the Planning–Implementing–Assessing cycle.
  3. Identify the essential characteristics of effective teachers, organized around Knowledge, Skills, and
     Dispositions.
  4. Compare the thoughts and actions of beginning versus experienced teachers across purpose,
     planning, teaching, assessment, and management.
  5. Explain what it means to treat a school subject as a discipline, and identify its structural elements:
     facts, concepts, principles, and skills.
  6. Describe Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) and distinguish it from content knowledge and
     general pedagogical knowledge.
  7. Explain the TPACK framework and identify its seven constituent knowledge domains.
  8. Define instructional design, identify its three core components, and compare the ADDIE, ASSURE,
     and Dick & Carey models.
  9. Apply the structure-of-knowledge and PCK concepts to concrete examples in IT, Science,
     Mathematics, and Art & Design.




                                                     3

Chapter One — Introduction to Teaching and the Subject as a Discipline




1. What Is Teaching?
Teaching can be defined as a deliberate, goal-directed process in which an educator organizes
experiences, resources, and interactions to help learners construct knowledge, develop skills, and form
attitudes they could not easily acquire on their own. Two ideas are central to this definition:

  • Intentionality — teaching is planned around specific outcomes rather than left to chance.
  • Facilitation — the teacher's role is to design and manage the conditions for learning, not merely to
    “transmit” facts from teacher to student.


1.1 Two Views of the Teacher's Role
It is useful to contrast two broad views of what a teacher does in the classroom:

                                          Primary source and deliverer of                 Relatively passive recipient of

                                                                                          Active builder of understanding
 Facilitation (constructivist-            Structures tasks, questions, and
                                                                                          through inquiry, discussion, and
 influenced) view                         environments that guide learning

Table 1.1. Two contrasting views of the teacher's instructional role.

Most contemporary methods courses — and the InTASC (Interstate Teacher Assessment and Support
Consortium) standards referenced throughout this course — favor a blend that leans toward facilitation
while still recognizing that direct explanation has an important place in effective teaching.

2. Basic Teaching Functions
Regardless of subject area, effective teachers repeatedly perform a set of core functions across the
instructional cycle. At the broadest level, these functions can be grouped into three overarching phases:

 Phase                       Description

                             Deciding about objectives, content, instructional strategies, student assessment,
 Planning
                             and related preparatory decisions.

                             The actual delivery of the plan — presenting content, questioning, and managing
 Implementing
                             the classroom in real time.

                             Determining the level of student learning achieved, and using that evidence to
 Assessing
                             judge progress and inform future teaching.

Table 2.1. The Planning–Implementing–Assessing macro-cycle of teaching.

At a more granular level, this macro-cycle unpacks into six recurring functions:

  • Planning — setting objectives, selecting content, sequencing activities, and choosing resources
    before instruction begins.
  • Presenting/Delivering — explaining, demonstrating, and modeling content clearly and at an
    appropriate pace.
  • Questioning — using questions to check understanding, provoke thinking, and guide discussion.
  • Managing — organizing time, materials, groupings, and behavior so that learning can proceed with
    minimal disruption.
  • Assessing — gathering evidence of learning during and after instruction to judge progress and
    adjust teaching.
  • Reflecting — reviewing what worked and what did not, and using that judgment to improve future
    lessons.
These functions are cyclical rather than strictly linear: assessment evidence from one lesson typically
feeds into the planning of the next, and reflection happens continuously, not only at the end of a unit.

3. Essential Characteristics of Effective Teachers
Research on teacher effectiveness — synthesized in widely used methods texts such as Burden and
Byrd's Methods for Effective Teaching (2019) — points to a recurring set of characteristics associated
with strong teaching. To promote student learning and achievement, effective teachers need well-
developed Knowledge, Skills, and Dispositions.


3.1 Knowledge, Skills, and Dispositions

 Domain                         What It Involves

                                The content the teacher teaches; education in general; general pedagogical
 1. Knowledge                   knowledge; Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK); and Technological
                                Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK).

 2. Skills
                                sometimes referred to as “performance.”

                                Values, commitment, and professional ethics; beliefs and attitudes that are
 3. Dispositions

Table 3.1. The three domains teachers draw on to promote student learning and achievement.


3.2 Research-Based Traits of Effective Teachers
Beyond this three-domain framework, effectiveness research also highlights specific observable traits:

  • Solid command of subject-matter content.
  • Clear, well-organized communication, both spoken and written.
  • Enthusiasm and genuine interest in the subject and in learners.
  • Fairness, warmth, and the ability to build rapport and trust with students.
  • Strong classroom management and organizational skills.
  • Flexibility — the ability to adjust plans in response to how a lesson is actually unfolding.
  • A reflective, improvement-oriented professional attitude.
None of these traits operates in isolation; effective teaching is the coordinated use of several of them at
once. Strong content knowledge without clear communication skills, for example, often fails to translate
into student learning — which leads directly to the concept of Pedagogical Content Knowledge
discussed in Section 6.

Taken together, Tables 4.1–4.5 illustrate a broader developmental pattern: experience tends to shift a

Chapter One — Introduction to Teaching and the Subject as a Discipline




5. The Subject as a Discipline
A discipline is more than a list of topics; it has its own structure of knowledge, made up of four
interrelated elements:

  • Facts — specific, verifiable pieces of information.
  • Concepts — categories or ideas that organize facts.
  • Principles or generalizations — rules or relationships that connect concepts.
  • Skills or processes — the discipline's characteristic ways of working (e.g., the scientific method in
    Science, algorithmic thinking in IT, proof and problem-solving in Mathematics, or the elements and
    principles of design in Art).
Thinking of a subject as a discipline, rather than a pile of facts to be covered, has direct consequences
for instructional planning: a teacher must decide not only what content to teach but which facts,
concepts, principles, and skills are most central, and in what order they should be built up so that later
ideas make sense in light of earlier ones.

6. Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK)
Lee Shulman (1986) introduced the influential idea of Pedagogical Content Knowledge to describe a
special kind of professional knowledge unique to teachers. It is distinct from (a) Content Knowledge —
knowing the subject matter itself — and (b) general Pedagogical Knowledge — knowing how to teach in
general, independent of subject. PCK is the blend of the two: knowing how to represent and explain a
specific idea in a specific subject so that particular learners can understand it, including awareness of
common misconceptions and the most effective analogies, examples, and representations for that
content.


6.1 Shulman's Knowledge Bases for Teaching

 Knowledge Type                           Description

                                          Deep understanding of the subject matter itself (facts, concepts,
 Content Knowledge
                                          principles).

                                          Broad principles of classroom management, instructional strategy,
 General Pedagogical Knowledge
                                          and learner development that apply across subjects.

 Pedagogical Content Knowledge

 (PCK)
                                          representations.

                                          Knowledge of the materials, programs, and sequencing designed to
 Curricular Knowledge

Table 6.1. Shulman's (1986) knowledge bases for teaching.


6.2 PCK in Practice Across Four Disciplines
  • IT — Students commonly confuse the assignment operator (=) with the equality operator (==).
    Strong PCK responds by introducing assignment first through a concrete analogy — ‘put this value
    into this labeled box’ — before ever showing a conditional statement that uses ==.
  • Science — Many students enter class believing heavier objects always fall faster. Strong PCK
    addresses this misconception directly, for example with a simulation showing a hammer and a
    feather falling at the same rate in a vacuum, before formally introducing Newton's second law.
  • Mathematics — Many students believe multiplication always makes numbers bigger. Strong PCK
    deliberately chooses an early example that multiplies by a fraction less than 1, so students confront
    and revise this misconception before it becomes an obstacle in later algebra.
  • Art & Design — Beginning students often equate ‘good art’ only with photographic realism. Strong
    PCK shows a deliberately curated range of abstract and stylized works early in the unit, broadening
    students’ criteria for quality before asking them to critique their own work.

7. Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK)
TPACK describes knowledge inside educators' minds that they draw on to make instructional decisions,
such as when they design lessons. Not all educators have the same TPACK, and teachers' knowledge —
including TPACK — is expected to develop with more teaching experience. It extends Shulman's PCK by
adding technology as a third interacting dimension alongside content and pedagogy, producing seven

7.2 How the Domains Converge
The three core circles — Pedagogical Knowledge (PK), Content Knowledge (CK), and Technological
Knowledge (TK) — overlap pairwise to form PCK (pedagogy + content), TCK (technology + content), and
TPK (technology + pedagogy). Where all three circles intersect lies TPACK itself: the simultaneous,
integrated consideration of subject-matter content, instructional pedagogy, student learning, and
technology, all situated within the particular classroom and school context in which the teacher works
(Kelly, 2008).

More transformative technology-supported lessons tend to place the technology directly in students'
hands, remain content-rich, and use technology to situate learning in ways that would be unattainable
without it. The more opportunities educators have to actively design, redesign, and enact such lessons,
the more their TPACK and technology-integration skills grow (Voogt et al., 2013).

8. Instructional Design
Instructional design is the practice of creating learning experiences to support learning. It is a systems
approach to analyzing, designing, developing, implementing, and evaluating any instructional experience
or learning product — including online courses, instructional manuals, video tutorials, and learning
simulations. More specifically, instructional design is the process of using knowledge of how people
learn to guide the choices of instructional sequences and strategies that meet the needs of learners and
desired learning outcomes.


8.1 Three Primary Components of Instructional Design
Although many models and theories guide instructional designers, instructional design practice calls for
all instruction to include three primary components:

  • Clear goals and objectives
  • Learning activities
  • Assessments


8.2 Instructional Design Models
8.2.1 ADDIE
ADDIE is one of the most well-recognized instructional design models. Founded in the 1970s at Florida
State University, ADDIE represents five phases considered foundational for almost any learning design
activity. The phases are typically drawn as a forward-moving sequence in which the final phase loops
back into the first, making ADDIE a continuous improvement cycle rather than a one-time procedure.




Figure 8.1. The ADDIE cycle: Analysis → Design → Development → Implementation → Evaluation, looping back into

9. Bringing the Concepts Together
The ideas developed in this chapter are cumulative rather than separate topics to be memorized in
isolation. Teaching begins with an intentional, facilitative stance (Section 1) and is carried out through
recurring functions of planning, implementing, and assessing (Section 2). Effective teachers bring
together knowledge, skill, and disposition (Section 3) in ways that visibly mature with experience
(Section 4). What a teacher plans for is not an arbitrary list of topics but a discipline with its own facts,
concepts, principles, and skills (Section 5), and knowing how to teach that discipline to particular
learners is the essence of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (Section 6). When technology becomes part
of the picture, PCK expands into TPACK (Section 7). Finally, instructional design provides the systematic
process — goals, activities, and assessments, organized through models such as ADDIE, ASSURE, or Dick
and Carey — through which all of the above is translated into an actual lesson or course (Section 8).

For postgraduate study, it is worth noting that these frameworks are not competing theories to be
chosen between, but complementary lenses: Shulman's PCK explains why subject-specific pedagogical
expertise matters; TPACK extends that explanation into technology-rich environments; and instructional
design models supply the concrete procedural steps for turning pedagogical judgment into a deliverable
learning experience.




                                                      19

Chapter One — Introduction to Teaching and the Subject as a Discipline




Chapter Summary
Teaching is an intentional, facilitative process built around a recurring cycle of planning, presenting,
questioning, managing, assessing, and reflecting. Effective teachers combine strong subject knowledge
with communication skills, management ability, fairness, and a reflective disposition — and these
qualities visibly develop as teachers move from beginning to experienced practice.

Treating a subject as a discipline — with its own facts, concepts, principles, and skills — rather than a list
of topics helps teachers plan more coherent instruction. Shulman's concept of Pedagogical Content
Knowledge captures the specialized expertise teachers need at the intersection of subject-matter
expertise and teaching skill; the TPACK framework extends this expertise into technology-integrated
teaching contexts. Instructional design, in turn, supplies the systematic process — clear goals, learning
activities, and assessments, organized through models such as ADDIE, ASSURE, or Dick and Carey — by
which this pedagogical knowledge is turned into effective lessons and courses. Together, these concepts
set the stage for the planning and standards topics covered in the next chapter.

TOPIC 2 · FOUNDATIONS OF INSTRUCTIONAL PLANNING AND PROFESSIONAL STANDARDS


Writing Measurable, Achievable Lesson
Objectives with the ABCD Model
A study reference for student teachers. Use it to plan your daily lessons, check your
objectives before you submit a plan, and revise for the topic assessment.

Learning outcomes
By the end of this topic, you will be able to:
  1. Explain how professional standards guide day-to-day planning decisions.
  2. Describe backward design as a way to align standards, objectives, and assessment.
  3. Identify the four parts of an ABCD objective: Audience, Behavior, Condition, and Degree.
  4. Write daily objectives that are measurable and achievable, and align them with activities and
     assessment.


Contents
1. How Professional Standards Guide Day-to-Day Planning ................................................................... 2
2. Backward Design: Start with the End in Mind .................................................................................... 3
3. The ABCD Model ................................................................................................................................. 4
4. Choosing Measurable Verbs ............................................................................................................... 5
5. Making Objectives Measurable and Achievable ................................................................................. 6
6. Writing an ABCD Objective Step by Step ............................................................................................ 8
7. Where Objectives Sit in the Daily Lesson Plan .................................................................................. 10
8. Practice and Self-Check ..................................................................................................................... 12
9. Summary, Key Terms, and References ............................................................................................. 14




                                                 Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 1

1. How Professional Standards Guide Day-to-Day Planning
Two kinds of standards shape every lesson you plan. Professional teaching standards describe what
a competent teacher does, including planning instruction from knowledge of content, learners, and
curriculum (for example, InTASC Standard 7, "Planning for Instruction"; use the standards that apply
in your own setting). Curriculum standards describe what students should know and be able to do.

 Type                          Answers the question                 Effect on your daily plan

 Professional teaching         How well do I plan and               Sets the quality bar: clear objectives,
 standards                     teach?                               planning for diverse learners, using
                                                                    assessment data, reflecting.

 Curriculum / content          What must students learn?            Every daily objective must trace back to a
 standards                                                          curriculum standard or learning outcome.




Infographic 1. The planning funnel. Standards are broad and long-term; a daily objective is one small, checkable step
                                                   toward them.


Daily decisions that standards inform

 Decision                           How the standard guides it

 What to teach today                The next manageable step toward the standard.

 How deep to go                     The verb in the standard (identify vs. analyze) tells you the thinking
                                    level.

 Which activities to use            Activities must practice the exact behavior named in the objective.

 How to check learning              The assessment must measure the objective, not something else.



                                      Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 2

Decision                         How the standard guides it

 How to differentiate             Professional standards expect you to plan supports for different
                                  learners.

 What to do tomorrow              Today's assessment results shape tomorrow's objective.




2. Backward Design: Start with the End in Mind
Backward design (Wiggins & McTighe, Understanding by Design) reverses the usual habit of choosing
activities first. You decide what students should learn, then how you will know they learned it, and
only then how you will teach it.




      Infographic 2. The three stages of backward design and what each one produces in a daily lesson plan.


 Stage                     Key question                             In a daily lesson plan

 1. Desired results        What should students know                Select the standard, then write the
                           and be able to do?                       ABCD objective(s).

 2. Acceptable             How will I know they have                Design the assessment. It must match
 evidence                  learned it?                              the objective's Behavior, Condition, and
                                                                    Degree.

 3. Learning plan          What teaching and practice will          Plan the introduction, modelling,
                           get them there?                          guided practice, and independent
                                                                    practice.


A well-written ABCD objective already contains its assessment. The Behavior says what students will
do, the Condition says the setting and tools, and the Degree gives the pass line. That is why objective
writing is the key skill in daily planning.




                                    Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 3

Infographic 3. The alignment triangle. If one side does not connect, the lesson is misaligned.


  Alignment test: read your objective, main activity, and assessment side by side. If a student does
  well in the activity, are they ready for the assessment? Does the assessment use the same
  behavior and conditions, at the stated level?




3. The ABCD Model
The ABCD model (from Heinich, Molenda, Russell & Smaldino, building on Mager) builds an objective
from four parts. Each part answers one question.




 Infographic 4. Anatomy of an ABCD objective. The order can change (the Condition often comes first), but all four
                                             parts should be there.




                                     Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 4

Part               Question              Guidance                                   Examples

 A · Audience       Who will learn?       Name the learners. Write about             Grade 3 students; Group
                                          the student, never the teacher.            B learners

 B · Behavior       What will they        One observable, measurable                 list, solve, compare, write
                    do?                   action verb plus the content. This
                                          is the most important part.

 C · Condition      Under what            What students are given, allowed           given a map; without a
                    circumstances?        to use, or limited by when they            calculator; after reading
                                          show the behavior.                         the text

 D · Degree         How well?             The success criterion: accuracy,           8 of 10; 80%; rubric level
                                          number correct, time limit, or             3; within 10 minutes
                                          rubric level.




4. Choosing Measurable Verbs
The Behavior verb decides whether an objective is measurable. Pick a verb you could see or hear a
student do, at the thinking level your standard asks for. The revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson &
Krathwohl) is a useful guide.




     Infographic 5. The Bloom's staircase: six levels of thinking, each with verbs you can observe and measure.


 Level               What students do                         Measurable verbs

 Remember            Recall facts and basic concepts          list, name, define, label, recall, match




                                     Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 5

Level              What students do                       Measurable verbs

 Understand         Explain ideas or concepts              explain, summarize, paraphrase, classify,
                                                           describe

 Apply              Use information in a new               solve, use, demonstrate, calculate, construct
                    situation

 Analyze            Break into parts, draw                 compare, contrast, categorize, distinguish,
                    connections                            organize

 Evaluate           Justify a decision or position         judge, justify, critique, defend, recommend

 Create             Produce new or original work           design, compose, write, plan, produce



Verbs to avoid in the Behavior
These describe what happens inside a student's head, so you cannot observe or measure them
directly: understand, know, learn, appreciate, be aware of, be familiar with, grasp, realize, believe.

  Fix: ask "What would I see or hear a student do to show they understand?" That action is your
  verb. Understand fractions becomes compare two fractions using <, >, or =.




5. Making Objectives Measurable and Achievable
Every daily objective must pass two tests. Measurable means you can see the learning and check it
against a clear standard. Achievable means your students, with what they already know, can
realistically reach it in one lesson with the resources you have.

 Is it MEASURABLE? Ask:                                 Is it ACHIEVABLE? Ask:

 • Can I see or hear the behavior?                      • Time: can students learn and show it within
 • Will students produce evidence: an answer,           the lesson?
 product, or performance?                               • Prior knowledge: do they have the skills it
 • Does the Degree have a number, criterion, or         builds on?
 rubric level?                                          • Scope: is it one step of the standard, not the
 • Would two teachers agree on whether a                whole unit?
 student met it?                                        • Degree: is the target realistic for a first
 • Can I check it by the end of the lesson?             attempt (often 70–80%, or 4 of 5)?
                                                        • Resources and learners: are the materials
                                                        available, and does it suit students' age,
                                                        language, and needs?




                                  Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 6

Infographic 6. The objective matrix. Aim for the top-right box every time.


How each ABCD part controls both qualities

 Part            Makes it measurable by…                         Makes it achievable by…

 Audience        Naming exactly whose performance                Reminding you to plan for these learners'
                 is checked.                                     level and needs.

 Behavior        Using an observable verb.                       Choosing a thinking level and amount of
                                                                 content that fits one lesson.

 Condition       Fixing the setting, so every student is         Adding supports (word bank, example,
                 judged the same way.                            manipulatives) that make a hard skill
                                                                 reachable.

 Degree          Giving a clear pass line (8 of 10, 80%,         Setting a realistic first-lesson target: not
                 rubric level 3).                                100%, and not so low it means nothing.



From unachievable to achievable

 Too much for one lesson            Why                       Achievable revision

 Grade 7 students will solve all    A whole unit;             Given ten one-step equations, Grade 7
 types of linear equations with     perfection on day         students will solve for the unknown with
 100% accuracy.                     one.                      at least 8 correct.




                                   Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 7

Too much for one lesson              Why                       Achievable revision

 Grade 5 students will design         Takes weeks, not          Given a research question, Grade 5
 and carry out a full                 one lesson.               students will identify the independent,
 investigation on plant                                         dependent, and controlled variables with
 growth.                                                        all three correct.

 Grade 10 students will               Too much                  After a guided reading of one poem, Grade
 critique five poems in 20            evaluation for the        10 students will justify their interpretation
 minutes.                             time.                     of its theme in a paragraph using at least
                                                                two quotations.

 Grade 2 students will write a        Beyond the age            Using a sentence frame and word bank,
 five-paragraph essay with no         level; 100% is            Grade 2 students will write three
 spelling errors.                     unrealistic.              sentences about a family member with a
                                                                capital letter and full stop in at least 2 of 3.



Break a standard into achievable daily steps
One broad standard usually needs several lessons. Make each day one achievable step. Over the
week, reduce the support and raise the thinking level.




   Infographic 7. The weekly staircase. Each daily objective is achievable, and together they reach the standard.



6. Writing an ABCD Objective Step by Step
 1. Start from the standard. Copy the curriculum standard or unit goal.


                                     Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 8

2. Choose today's step. What part can students realistically achieve in this lesson?
 3. Name the Audience: who are the learners?
 4. Select the Behavior: one measurable verb at the right level, plus the content.
 5. Set the Condition: what students are given, may use, or are limited by.
 6. Define the Degree: a realistic, checkable pass line.
 7. Read it aloud. Is it one clear sentence that another teacher would assess the same way?
 8. Write the assessment from it. If you cannot, revise the objective.

Worked example: Grade 7 Mathematics

 Step                    Decision

 Standard                Solve real-world problems involving ratios and rates.

 Today's step            Use unit rates to compare prices.

 Audience                Grade 7 students

 Behavior                calculate unit prices and decide which is the better buy (Apply)

 Condition               given five pairs of supermarket price labels and a calculator

 Degree                  correctly for at least 4 of the 5 pairs

 Objective               Given five pairs of price labels and a calculator, Grade 7 students will
                         calculate unit prices and decide which is the better buy correctly for at
                         least 4 of the 5 pairs.

 Aligned assessment      An exit ticket with five new pairs of price labels. Students show the
                         calculation and circle the better buy.



Weak vs. strong objectives

 Weak                        Problem                      Strong ABCD version

 Students will understand    Vague verb; no               Using a labelled diagram, Grade 6 students
 photosynthesis.             condition or degree.         will explain the inputs and outputs of
                                                          photosynthesis, naming all three inputs and
                                                          both outputs.

 The teacher will show       Describes the                Given a graphic organizer, Grade 3 students
 how to write a              teacher, not the             will write a paragraph with a topic sentence,
 paragraph.                  learner.                     three details, and a closing sentence,
                                                          including all five parts.




                                 Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 9

Weak                         Problem                     Strong ABCD version

 Students will complete       An activity, not a          Without a calculator, Grade 4 students will
 page 45.                     learning outcome.           multiply two-digit by one-digit numbers with
                                                          at least 80% accuracy.

 Students will know the       Vague and too broad         Given ten sentences, Grade 2 students will
 parts of speech.             for one lesson.             underline the noun and circle the verb in
                                                          each with at least 8 correct.



Common mistakes
  • Writing what the teacher will do instead of the student.
  • Writing an activity ("complete the worksheet") instead of a learning outcome.
  • Using vague verbs such as understand, know, or learn.
  • Putting several behaviors in one objective. Write separate objectives.
  • A Degree you cannot check ("will do well").
  • A Condition that does not match the assessment ("using a calculator" when the quiz bans
    them).
  • An objective that is too big for one lesson, or a Degree of 100% on a first attempt.



7. Where Objectives Sit in the Daily Lesson Plan
The objective goes near the top of the plan, and every later section links back to it. Most lessons
need one to three objectives. The letters show which ABCD part each section depends on.




                                 Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 10

Infographic 8. The lesson plan flow, showing which ABCD part each section depends on.


Turn the objective into a student-friendly target

 For                       Wording

 Your plan                 Given five pairs of price labels and a calculator, Grade 7 students will
                           calculate unit prices and decide which is the better buy correctly for at
                           least 4 of the 5 pairs.

 Students ("I can")        "I can find the price of one item so I can tell which deal is better."

 Success criterion         "I get at least 4 out of 5 right on my exit ticket."




                                   Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 11

8. Practice and Self-Check

Objective planning template
Use this template to draft each objective for your lesson plan.

 Part                           Your decision

 content)

Quick quiz: what is the problem?
Decide whether each objective is (a) measurable and achievable, (b) not measurable, or (c) not
achievable.
  1. Students will understand the causes of World War I.
  2. Given ten one-step equations, Grade 7 students will solve for x with at least 8 correct.
  3. Grade 1 students will read a 300-word story aloud with no errors.
  4. The teacher will explain the rules for adding fractions.
  5. Grade 5 students will design, carry out, and report a full science investigation in one lesson.

Activity 1: Label the parts
Mark A, B, C, and D in each objective.




                                 Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 12

1. Using a ruler, Grade 3 students will measure the length of five classroom objects to the
    nearest centimetre.
 2. After reading the story, students will sequence six events in the correct order with no errors.
 3. Grade 8 students will write a persuasive letter of at least 200 words, using the checklist
    provided, scoring 3 or higher on the rubric.

Activity 2: From standard to daily objectives
Choose a curriculum standard from your specialization. Using backward design, write:
 1. Two ABCD objectives at different Bloom's levels for one lesson.
 2. An aligned assessment for each objective.
 3. One main activity for each objective.
 4. One sentence naming the professional teaching standard your plan shows, and how.

Self-check before you submit a lesson plan

 ✓      Criterion

 ☐      It links to a specific curriculum standard or learning outcome.

 ☐      A: it names the learners and focuses on the student, not the teacher.

 ☐      B: it uses one observable verb at the right thinking level.

 ☐      C: it states the materials, setting, or limits, and these match the assessment.

 ☐      D: it states a clear, realistic success criterion.

 ☐      It describes a learning outcome, not an activity.

 ☐      Measurable: I know exactly what evidence I will collect and what counts as success.

 ☐      Achievable: it fits the lesson time, builds on prior knowledge, and sets a realistic Degree.

 ☐      Another teacher could assess it the same way I would.



Answer key
Quick quiz
 1. (b) Not measurable. "Understand" cannot be observed. Try: "Given a timeline, Grade 9
    students will explain three causes of World War I, with a supporting fact for each."
 2. (a) Measurable and achievable. All four parts are present, the verb is observable, and 8 of 10
    is a realistic target.
 3. (c) Not achievable. The text is too long and "no errors" is unrealistic for Grade 1. Try a 50-word
    decodable text with at least 90% of words read correctly.


                                   Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 13

4. (b) Not measurable. It describes the teacher, not the students.
  5. (c) Not achievable. Three large behaviors in one lesson. Break it into daily steps across the
     week.
Activity 1
  1. C: using a ruler · A: Grade 3 students · B: measure the length of five objects · D: to the
     nearest centimetre
  2. C: after reading the story · A: students · B: sequence six events · D: in the correct order with
     no errors
  3. A: Grade 8 students · B: write a persuasive letter · C: using the checklist provided · D: at least
     200 words, rubric level 3 or higher



9. Summary, Key Terms, and References

Summary
  • Professional standards set how well you plan; curriculum standards set what students learn.
  • Daily objectives break broad standards into small, measurable steps.
  • Backward design: results (objective) first, then evidence (assessment), then learning
    experiences (activities).
  • ABCD: Audience, Behavior, Condition, Degree.
  • A strong objective is measurable (observable verb and clear pass line) and achievable (one
    realistic step for these students in one lesson).

Key terms

 Term                         Meaning

 Alignment                    The match between standards, objectives, activities, and assessment.

 Backward design              Planning that starts from desired results and evidence before
                              choosing activities.

 Learning objective           A statement of what learners will be able to do by the end of a lesson.

 Measurable verb              An action verb describing performance you can observe.

 Achievable                   Realistic for these learners, in this time, with these resources.

 Success criterion            The level of performance that shows the objective was met (the
                              Degree).




                                 Topic 2 · Writing ABCD Objectives · Page 14

References
Anderson, L. W., & Krathwohl, D. R. (Eds.). (2001). A taxonomy for learning, teaching, and assessing:
       A revision of Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives. Longman.

        progressions for teachers 1.0. CCSSO.
Heinich, R., Molenda, M., Russell, J. D., & Smaldino, S. E. (2002). Instructional media and
        technologies for learning (7th ed.). Merrill/Prentice Hall.
Mager, R. F. (1997). Preparing instructional objectives (3rd ed.). Center for Effective Performance.
Wiggins, G., & McTighe, J. (2005). Understanding by design (Expanded 2nd ed.). ASCD.

TOPIC 3

 Instructional Planning: Foundations, Levels & the Daily
                       Lesson Plan
                                Methods of Teaching – Foundational Concepts


Learning Objectives
By the end of this study guide, you should be able to:

    •   Define instructional planning and explain why it is essential to effective teaching.
    •   Describe the four organizing categories of the InTASC Model Core Teaching Standards.
    •   Identify the major subject-specific standards frameworks for IT, Science, Mathematics, and Art &
        Design.
    •   Identify the levels of planning, from yearly/course plans down to daily lesson plans, and
        distinguish long-range from short-range planning.
    •   List common resources teachers use when planning instruction.
    •   Describe the essential components of a written lesson plan and their purpose.
    •   Explain how planning differs across the cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains.

  Builds on Topic 2: Writing ABCD objectives, choosing measurable verbs, making objectives
  measurable and achievable, backward design, and aligning objectives with activities and assessment
  are covered in Topic 2 and are not repeated here.



Part A: Foundations of Instructional Planning

1. What Is Instructional Planning?
Instructional planning is the process by which a teacher decides, in advance, what students should learn,
how that learning will be organized and delivered, and how it will be assessed. A plan translates broad
goals (a curriculum standard, a unit theme) into concrete decisions about content, sequencing, activities,
materials, grouping, and time. Planning happens at several levels, from a whole-year overview down to a
single lesson (see Part B), but at every level its purpose is the same: to make teaching purposeful and
coherent rather than improvised.

2. Why Planning Matters
    •   Curriculum coverage – a plan helps a teacher pace content so that all required standards are
        addressed within the available time.
    •   Anticipation – planning allows a teacher to foresee likely student difficulties, prepare materials,
        and think through classroom-management issues before they occur.


                                    Topic 3 – Instructional Planning | Page 1

•   Differentiation – advance planning creates room to design alternative tasks or supports for
        learners with different needs.
    •   Coherence – planning keeps the parts of a lesson connected to one another and to the larger
        unit, rather than a list of separate activities.
    •   Professional accountability – clear plans make a teacher’s instructional decisions visible and
        defensible to supervisors, colleagues, and families.

3. The InTASC Model Core Teaching Standards
The Interstate Teacher Assessment and Support Consortium (InTASC), coordinated by the Council of Chief
State School Officers (CCSSO, 2013), publishes a widely adopted set of ten standards describing what
effective teachers should know and be able to do. Originally written for beginning teachers, the standards
were revised in 2011 to apply to teachers at every stage of their careers. The ten standards are grouped
into four categories.

Key Framework: InTASC Model Core Teaching Standards (CCSSO, 2013)
 Category                      Standards         Focus

 The Learner and Learning      1–3               Learner development, learning differences, and creating
                                                 a supportive learning environment.

 Content                       4–5               Deep content knowledge and the ability to apply it,
                                                 connecting concepts and perspectives to engage learners
                                                 in critical thinking and problem solving.

 Instructional Practice        6–8               Assessment, planning for instruction, and using varied
                                                 instructional strategies.

 Professional Responsibility   9–10              Professional learning and ethical practice; leadership and
                                                 collaboration with colleagues, families, and the
                                                 community.


These categories give teachers a shared professional language that recurs throughout this course:
planning (this topic), instructional strategies, and assessment all belong to the Instructional Practice
category.




                                     Topic 3 – Instructional Planning | Page 2

4. Subject-Specific Standards Frameworks
Each discipline also has its own standards framework. These are the main frameworks for the four
specializations in this course:

 Specialization   Framework                            Main Emphasis

 IT               ISTE Standards (International        The Standards for Educators guide the effective
                  Society for Technology in            use of digital tools in teaching; the Standards for
                  Education)                           Students describe learner roles (e.g.,
                                                       Computational Thinker) that educators plan
                                                       toward.

 Mathematics      NCTM Principles and                  Content standards plus five process standards:
                  Standards for School                 problem solving, reasoning and proof,
                  Mathematics                          communication, connections, and
                                                       representation.

 Science          National Science Education           Science content expectations; the NSES
                  Standards (NSES) / Next              emphasized inquiry, which the NGSS frames as
                  Generation Science Standards         science and engineering practices (e.g., asking
                  (NGSS)                               questions, planning and carrying out
                                                       investigations).

 Art & Design     National Core Arts Standards         Four artistic processes: Creating;
                                                       Performing/Presenting/Producing; Responding;
                                                       and Connecting.




                                 Topic 3 – Instructional Planning | Page 3

Part B: Levels and Types of Planning

5. Levels of Planning
Instructional planning is organized into a hierarchy that moves from broad and long-term to specific and
immediate (Burden & Byrd, 2019). Each level works within the limits set by the broader level before it and
narrows the focus.

Key Framework: The Planning Hierarchy
 Level                          Time Span                    Purpose

 Yearly / Course Plan           One academic year or         Maps major units and standards across the entire
                                course                       course; ensures full curriculum coverage.

 Term Plan                      One semester or              Divides the yearly plan into the units and topics to
                                term                         be completed within a single term.

 Unit Plan                      Several weeks                Organizes a coherent block of related lessons
                                                             around a shared theme, concept, or set of
                                                             standards.

 Weekly Plan                    One week                     Distributes the unit’s lessons across the days of
                                                             the week and schedules activities, assessments,
                                                             and materials.

 Daily Lesson Plan              One class session            Details the objectives, activities, timing of each
                                                             step, and assessment for a single teaching period.




         Figure 1. The Planning Pyramid: each level works within the boundaries of the broader level beneath it.




                                        Topic 3 – Instructional Planning | Page 4

6. Types of Planning: Long-Range vs. Short-Range
                        Long-Range Planning                            Short-Range Planning

 Levels covered         Yearly, term, and unit plans                   Weekly and daily lesson plans

 Main decisions         Curriculum mapping, pacing guides,             Specific activities, questions,
                        and which standards are taught when            materials, and time allocations for
                                                                       each class session

 How often revised      A few times per term                           Continuously, often daily, based on
                                                                       how earlier lessons went and what
                                                                       assessment evidence shows

 Metaphor               Sets the map                                   Fills in the route



7. Resources for Planning
Effective planning draws on several sources of information rather than a single textbook:

    •   Official curriculum frameworks and the subject-specific standards in Section 4.
    •   Approved textbooks and their accompanying teacher’s guides.
    •   Prior student assessment data, used to identify gaps or misconceptions to address.
    •   Colleagues and mentor teachers, through collaborative planning or lesson study.
    •   Professional and digital repositories of vetted lesson materials, simulations, and activities.
    •   Reflections from previous deliveries of the same lesson or unit.




Part C: The Daily Lesson Plan

8. Components of a Written Lesson Plan
While formats vary by institution, most lesson plans share a common set of components, each serving a
distinct purpose (Borich, 2017).




                                    Topic 3 – Instructional Planning | Page 5

Key Framework: Standard Lesson Plan Components
 Component                             Purpose

 Objectives                            State what students will be able to do by the end of the lesson
                                       (see Topic 2).

 Materials / Resources                 List everything needed to deliver the lesson (equipment,
                                       handouts, technology).

 Opening / Set Induction               Capture attention and connect new content to prior
                                       knowledge.

 Development / Procedures              Sequence the main teaching and learning activities step by
                                       step.

 Guided / Independent Practice         Give students opportunities to apply the new content with
                                       decreasing support.

 Assessment / Check for                Gather evidence that the objectives were met, during or at the
 Understanding                         end of the lesson.

 Closure                               Summarize key learning and preview what comes next.

 Differentiation Notes                 Describe adjustments for learners with different needs or
                                       readiness levels.



9. Planning for the Three Learning Domains
Lesson objectives can target one or more of three domains of learning. Each domain calls for different
planning decisions (each domain and its taxonomy is examined in depth in a later topic).

 Domain             Type of Learning                              Planning Implications

 Cognitive          Knowledge and intellectual skills             Plan explanations, examples,
                    (recalling, explaining, analyzing)            questioning, and problem-solving tasks.

 Affective          Attitudes, values, and feelings               Plan discussion, reflection, and
                    (valuing, willingly participating)            opportunities for students to make and
                                                                  justify choices.

 Psychomotor        Physical or manual skills (operating          Plan demonstration, enough hands-on
                    equipment, executing a technique)             practice time, materials for every
                                                                  student, and safety steps.




                                   Topic 3 – Instructional Planning | Page 6

Applying This Topic Across the Four Specializations
The same planning structure looks different once it is filled with real subject content. For each
specialization below, a subject standard is turned into a planning decision, followed by a sample unit,
lesson, set induction, and planning resources.

IT
 Planning Element          Example

 Standard in action        ISTE Standards for Students – Computational Thinker. A lesson on a new
                           programming topic does not start with syntax alone; students first break a
                           real-world task (e.g., “plan the steps to make a cup of tea”) into an ordered
                           sequence of instructions before the matching code structure is introduced.

 Unit / Lesson             Programming Fundamentals / Introduction to Conditional Statements

 Set induction             Present a real-life if/then scenario (“If it rains, I bring an umbrella”) and ask
                           students to phrase two of their own before naming the coding structure.

 Key resources             ISTE Standards documents; a simple flowchart template



Science
 Planning Element          Example

 Standard in action        NSES / NGSS – inquiry and science practices. Rather than only lecturing
                           about photosynthesis, a teacher plans a plant-growth lesson around a
                           testable question (“Does the amount of sunlight affect how tall a bean
                           plant grows?”) and has students propose a hypothesis and a simple
                           experimental design.

 Unit / Lesson             Ecosystems / Food Chains and Food Webs

 Set induction             Give students cards naming local organisms and ask them to physically
                           arrange a chain from producer to top predator.

 Key resources             NSES/NGSS documents; local food-web diagrams

Mathematics
 Planning Element          Example

 Standard in action        NCTM Process Standard – Problem Solving. A teacher covering percentages
                           opens with an authentic, under-specified problem (“Which of these three
                           stores offers the best real discount?”) and lets students choose their own
                           strategy before formally naming the procedure.

 Unit / Lesson             Linear Equations / Slope-Intercept Form

 Set induction             Show a graph comparing the cost of two phone plans over time and ask
                           which plan is cheaper after six months.

 Key resources             NCTM standards document; graphing calculator or graphing app



Art & Design
 Planning Element          Example

 Standard in action        National Core Arts Standards – Creating (Anchor Standard 1: generate and
                           conceptualize artistic ideas and work). A teacher planning a painting unit
                           requires a page of thumbnail sketches before students touch paint, so
                           each final piece reflects the student’s own idea rather than a teacher-
                           dictated design.

 Unit / Lesson             Color Theory / Complementary Colors

 Set induction             Display two paintings side by side, one using complementary colors and
                           one not, and ask students which feels more vivid and why.

 Key resources             National Core Arts Standards document; a physical color wheel



Summary
   •   Instructional planning turns broad goals into coherent, teachable sequences of content, activity,
       and assessment; it supports curriculum coverage, anticipation, differentiation, coherence, and
       accountability.
   •   InTASC groups its ten teaching standards into four categories: the Learner and Learning,
       Content, Instructional Practice, and Professional Responsibility.
   •   Each specialization has its own framework: ISTE (IT), NCTM (Mathematics), NSES/NGSS
       (Science), and the National Core Arts Standards (Art & Design).
   •   Planning happens at nested levels: yearly/course, term, unit, weekly, and daily. Long-range
       planning sets the map; short-range planning fills in the route.



                                  Topic 3 – Instructional Planning | Page 8

•   Good plans draw on several resources: standards, textbooks, assessment data, colleagues,
        repositories, and reflection.
    •   A written lesson plan includes objectives, materials, opening, development, practice,
        assessment, closure, and differentiation, and its activities should suit the domain (cognitive,
        affective, or psychomotor) being targeted.
